analysis.one_liner: Eases Dodd-Frank "skin in the game" rules for managers of corporate-loan investment funds.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on it: introduced in September 2017 with one Democratic cosponsor, the bill sat in the Financial Services Committee until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, firms that bundle loans into securities for investors must keep 5% of the credit risk on their own books — the "skin in the game" rule meant to make bundlers careful about loan quality. This bill would let certain bundles of corporate loans, called collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), satisfy that rule a different way: the fund's manager, or its affiliates and employees, could hold 5% of the fund's equity instead. The bill also sets detailed conditions for these funds — limits on loan quality, concentration, and monthly disclosure to investors. It was introduced and referred to committee, and no vote ever happened.
analysis.who_benefits: CLO fund managers and the banks and dealers that arrange syndicated corporate loans gain if the bill passes: securitizing those loans becomes cheaper and easier because the originating bank no longer has to hold 5% of the credit risk itself, and the manager's stake is a lighter, cheaper form of compliance. The bill's stated premise is that easier CLO issuance expands lending to mid-sized companies that borrow through the syndicated loan market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Loan-bundle managers and Wall Street securitizers

how_it_helps.text: Lets a "qualified" collateralized loan obligation meet the 5% risk-retention requirement by having the fund manager — or its majority-owned affiliates, knowledgeable employees, and other employees — buy and hold at least 5% of the fund's equity, with 70% of that in equity securities and no hedging, rather than by having the loan originator retain the risk.

Attaches conditions to qualify: at least 100% of assets in senior secured loans and cash, no defaulted assets or derivatives, no more than 60% covenant-lite loans (loans with few borrower protections), no more than 3.5% exposure to any single borrower or 15% to any single industry, and an equity cushion of at least 8% of assets.

Requires the manager to be an SEC-registered investment adviser, subordinates a majority of manager fees to payments owed on the fund's debt, limits discretionary asset sales to 30% of principal per year, and mandates monthly asset-level reporting to holders of the fund's debt securities.
The Congressional Research Service describes the bill as revising risk-retention requirements applicable to certain asset-backed securities.

analysis.who_pays: The cost of the weakened safeguard is diffuse. The risk-retention rule existed because securitizations with poorly underwritten loans amplified the 2008 financial crisis; shifting retention from the loan originator to the fund manager means that when corporate loans sour, more of the losses land on investors in the securities — and because qualified investors include qualified purchasers such as pension funds, retirement savings can end up holding that risk. Corporate borrowers whose loans are of lower quality could also face easier credit on riskier terms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors in the securities, including pension funds

drawbacks.text: It loosens Dodd-Frank's core safeguard: the originating bank no longer must hold 5% of the credit risk of loans it makes, so lenders can offload risk onto securities investors, and qualified investors include qualified purchasers — a category that includes pension funds — putting ordinary retirement savings in the path of any losses.

It permits up to 60% of a qualifying fund's assets to be covenant-lite loans, which carry few financial protections for lenders; the bill itself treats these as riskier enough to require quarterly unaudited and annual audited borrower financials as a condition.

The risk-retention rule was a post-2008 response to securitization markets that packaged and sold loans with little underwriting discipline; carving out a large, fast-growing loan-securitization category weakens that discipline even with the bill's other conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a targeted rollback with a real argument behind it. Supporters, including the bill's Democratic cosponsor, could argue that manager-held equity plus the bill's asset-quality, concentration, and transparency tests give investors better information and alignment than a rigid 5% originator-retention rule — the title's claim is that this financing is \"proven.\" The counterweight is that the bill's whole effect is to reduce who bears credit risk when corporate loans are packaged and sold, the exact mechanism that spread losses in 2008, and it opens the door wider to covenant-lite lending. On balance, the bill's benefits flow mainly to loan-bundle managers and securitization desks, while the added risk — if the safeguards prove insufficient — falls on investors, including retirement money, and potentially on the broader economy in a downturn.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never got a committee vote or floor action before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Andy Barr (R-KY) introduced the bill on September 14, 2017, joined by Representative David Scott (D-GA).
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services.
That was the only action ever taken: the bill received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The Congressional Research Service summary notes the bill would revise risk-retention requirements applicable to certain asset-backed securities.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Dodd-Frank skin-in-the-game framework for loan securitizations stayed as it was; loan-bundle managers and securitizers did not get the statutory carve-out they sought, and the existing risk-retention structure was not weakened.

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through introduction.

for.name: Rep. David Scott
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Took the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill and a Democrat cosponsored it, but no votes were ever recorded, so support never faced a partisan test.

industries.note: The bill lets the fund manager or its affiliates and employees satisfy the 5% risk-retention requirement by holding the fund's equity, a cheaper and lighter form of compliance than the Dodd-Frank rule's design. Their gain comes from reducing the skin-in-the-game safeguard, with the shifted risk landing on securities investors.

industries.industry: Banks and dealers in the leveraged loan market
industries.note: Easier CLO issuance means more demand for syndicated corporate loans and more securitization fees, while originating banks no longer have to retain 5% of the credit risk of loans they make. The benefit to lenders comes with less of the loss exposure the 2010 law required them to keep.

industries.industry: Mid-sized companies that borrow through syndicated loans
industries.note: The bill's premise is that easier loan-bundle issuance keeps credit flowing to employers that borrow in the syndicated loan market. The connection is indirect: the bill changes securitization rules, not lending terms, and easier credit can also fund riskier deals.

Qualified investors include qualified purchasers such as pension funds, so these investors get more product options plus the bill's monthly asset-level disclosure. The same change means retirement money could more readily hold the credit risk that originating banks no longer retain.
